We Still Don’t Understand High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

 

Colin Doumont∗*          Donney Fan          Natalie Maus Tübingen AI Center c.doumont@uni-tuebingen.de          University of British Columbia Vector Institute          University of Pennsylvania

Jacob R. Gardner          Henry Moss          Geoff Pleiss University of Pennsylvania          Lancaster University University of Cambridge          University of British Columbia Vector Institute

https://github.com/colmont/linear-bo

Abstract

Existing high-dimensional Bayesian optimization (BO) methods aim to overcome the curse of dimensionality by carefully encoding structural assumptions, from locality to sparsity to smoothness, into the optimization procedure. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that these approaches are outperformed by arguably the simplest method imaginable: Bayesian linear regression. After applying a geometric transformation to avoid boundary-seeking behavior, Gaussian processes with linear kernels match state-of-the-art performance on tasks with 60- to 6,000-dimensional search spaces. Linear models offer numerous advantages over their non-parametric counterparts: they afford closed-form sampling and their computation scales linearly with data, a fact we exploit on molecular optimization tasks with >>\penalty\ 20,000 observations. Coupled with empirical analyses, our results suggest the need to depart from past intuitions about BO methods in high-dimensions.

1 INTRODUCTION

High-dimensional search spaces have historically been a challenge for Bayesian optimization (BO). Classic theoretical results demonstrate that regret increases exponentially with dimensionality (Srinivas et al.,, 2010; Bull,, 2011) and naïve BO implementations can even perform worse than random search on problems exceeding 10 dimensions (Wang et al.,, 2016; Santoni et al.,, 2024). The most successful high-dimensional BO algorithms have exploited or imposed structural assumptions on the problem’s objective function, such as additive decompositions (Kandasamy et al.,, 2015; Gardner et al.,, 2017; Mutny and Krause,, 2018; Wang et al.,, 2018), locality (Eriksson et al.,, 2019; Müller et al.,, 2021; Wu et al.,, 2023), geometric warpings (Oh et al.,, 2018; Kirschner et al.,, 2019), or sparsity (Eriksson and Jankowiak,, 2021; Papenmeier et al.,, 2022). These approaches achieve better performance than naïve methods and even offer asymptotic reductions in regret under appropriate structural conditions (Kandasamy et al.,, 2015; Wu et al.,, 2023). Nevertheless, these algorithms are often complicated, introduce many hyperparameters, and may require many observations for meaningful optimization.

11footnotetext: Work done while at the Vector Institute.

Recently, Hvarfner et al., (2024) and Xu et al., (2025) achieved breakthrough results on high-dimensional problems without any structural assumptions, relying only on Gaussian process priors that favor simple functions as dimensionality DD increases. Specifically, after scaling kernel lengthscale hyperparameters proportionally to D\sqrt{D} to encourage smoothness, they show that the decades-old “Vanilla” BO recipe—expected improvement using a Gaussian process with a squared-exponential kernel (Močkus,, 1974; Jones et al.,, 1998)—achieves competitive performance across problems up to D>6000D>6000. Perhaps most remarkably, they demonstrate empirical success in a seemingly intractable regime, where the observation budget NN is on the same order as the search space dimensionality DD (which we denote by N≈DN\approx D). With N≈DN\approx D, one cannot even build a first-order Taylor approximation around a single point (i.e. a locally linear model), and yet Vanilla BO outperforms methods specifically engineered for high-dimensional problems.

Recognizing that true global optimization is all but impossible when N≈DN\approx D, we push this smoothness approach to its logical extreme. Specifically, we restrict the surrogate model to only have support for linear functions, the smoothest functions under most mathematical definitions. With linear models, we can globally model linear functions or locally model non-linear functions, but not both. Nevertheless, we hypothesize that the simplicity of these models may be beneficial, particularly in the N≈DN\approx D regime. Specifically, if observation budgets cannot support learning beyond locally-linear approximations, we hypothesize that simple Bayesian linear surrogate models are viable alternatives to non-parametric Gaussian processes. Linear models could also prove valuable in the N≫DN\gg D setting: their O⁡(D)O(D) parametric representation affords closed-form sampling and O⁡(N​D2)O(ND^{2}) computational complexity, whereas their non-degenerate Gaussian process counterparts require O⁡(N3)O(N^{3}) computation and do not admit exact pathwise samples.

Standard BO references do not recommend the use of linear models, or equivalently Gaussian processes with linear kernels (Frazier,, 2018; Garnett,, 2023). Indeed, our own experiments show that linear kernels in their most naïve form perform extremely poorly on most high-dimensional BO tasks (see Figure 2). However, our analyses reveal that this poor performance is largely attributable to boundary-seeking behavior of linear models, which we address through simple geometric modifications to the kernel. Our most significant proposal is to bijectively map the input space (typically a hypercube in ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}) onto a hypersphere in ℝD+1\mathbb{R}^{D+1}, yielding provable immunity from boundary-seeking behavior and resulting in a kernel that is a function of cosine similarity between pairs of inputs.

Surprisingly, while standard linear kernels fail to yield meaningful optimization, our spherically-projected linear kernels match or exceed state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks from D=60D=60 to D>6000D>6000. Most notably, our sphere-domain linear models excel when N≫DN\gg D and exact Gaussian process inference becomes computationally prohibitive, providing a significant performance improvement over existing scalable approaches like stochastic variational Gaussian processes (Hensman et al.,, 2013; Vakili et al.,, 2021; Moss et al.,, 2023). Beyond demonstrating the state-of-the-art performance of our spherically-projected linear kernels, especially in large-NN settings, these results further question our understanding of high-dimensional Bayesian optimization. The fact that the simplest possible surrogate model (after correcting for geometric pathologies) can match or outperform all other methods suggests the need for a radical departure from the conventional wisdom and theory in the field.

2 BACKGROUND & RELATED WORK

2.1 Bayesian Optimization

The goal of Bayesian optimization (Garnett,, 2023) is to find the global optimum 𝐱∗∈𝒳\mathbf{x}^{*}\in\mathcal{X} of a black-box function f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, where ff can only be evaluated point-wise and those evaluations are considered “expensive” (e.g. in time or money). Depending on the setting, these evaluations of ff can also be noisy, i.e. f⁡(𝐱)+εif(\mathbf{x})+\varepsilon_{i} with εi∼𝒩⁡(0,σε2)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}\right). Although 𝒳\mathcal{X} can represent different spaces, the typical space in BO is the unit hypercube, i.e. 𝒳=[0,1]D\mathcal{X}=[0,1]^{D}. In this paper, we consider the centered hypercube [−1,1]D[-1,1]^{D}, which can easily be mapped to or from [0,1]D[0,1]^{D}.

To find 𝐱∗\mathbf{x^{*}}, BO iteratively selects new points at which to evaluate ff, where these points are chosen by maximizing an acquisition function αt​(⋅)\alpha_{t}(\cdot), i.e. 𝐱t+1=arg⁡max𝐱∈𝒳​αt​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\alpha_{t}(\mathbf{x}), which balances exploration and exploitation by relying on a (probabilistic) surrogate model of ff, for example a Gaussian process (GP).

Gaussian Processes.

GPs define distributions over functions that are specified by a mean function μ⁡(𝐱)\mu(\mathbf{x}) (typically a constant) and a covariance function or kernel k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′):𝒳×𝒳→ℝk(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x^{\prime}}):\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. GPs can be equivalently viewed as Bayesian linear regression with a (potentially infinite-dimensional) basis expansion, where k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x^{\prime}}) corresponds to the inner product under this featurization. It is common to use kernels that correspond to infinite-dimensional basis expansions, such as the Radial Basis Function (RBF):

kRBF​(𝐱,𝐱′):=exp⁡(−12​‖𝐳−𝐳′‖2),\displaystyle k_{\textrm{RBF}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}):=\exp\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lVert\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z^{\prime}}\right\rVert^{2}\right),
𝐳:=[x1ℓ1⋯xDℓD],𝐳′:=[x1′ℓ1⋯xD′ℓD].\displaystyle\mathbf{z}:=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{x_{1}}{\ell_{1}}&\cdots&\tfrac{x_{D}}{\ell_{D}}\end{bmatrix},\quad\mathbf{z^{\prime}}:=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{x^{\prime}_{1}}{\ell_{1}}&\cdots&\tfrac{x^{\prime}_{D}}{\ell_{D}}\end{bmatrix}.

Here, the lengthscales ℓi>0\ell_{i}>0 are hyperparameters that re-scale the search space 𝒳\mathcal{X} before applying the kernel. Recent work has shown the necessity of scaling these lengthscales with D\sqrt{D}, so that the expected norms of the re-scaled inputs 𝐳\mathbf{z}, 𝐳′\mathbf{z}^{\prime} are independent of dimensionality (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024; Xu et al.,, 2025; Papenmeier et al., 2025b, ).

Degenerate Kernels and Linear Models.

While kernels corresponding to infinite basis expansions (e.g. the RBF kernel) often yield universally approximating functions, kernels corresponding to finite basis expansions have limited representational capacity. In particular, the linear kernel, defined as

klinear​(𝐱,𝐱′):=b0+b1​𝐱⊤​𝐱′k_{\mathrm{linear}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}):=b_{0}+b_{1}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{x^{\prime}} (1)

for some hyperparameters b0,b1>0b_{0},b_{1}>0, only corresponds to the (D+1D+1)-dimensional basis expansion [b0,b1​x1,…,b1​xD][\sqrt{b_{0}},\sqrt{b_{1}}x_{1},\ldots,\sqrt{b_{1}}x_{D}]. Similarly, polynomial kernels of the form (b0+b1​𝐱⊤​𝐱′)m\left(b_{0}+b_{1}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\right)^{m} with m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} correspond to O⁡(Dm)O(D^{m})-dimensional basis expansions. Usually, these kernels are avoided for BO in favor of their universal approximating counterparts (Garnett,, 2023).

2.2 High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

Classic results show that the regret of BO with universally approximating kernels increases exponentially with DD (Srinivas et al.,, 2010; Bull,, 2011), and thus problems with ≥20\geq 20 dimensions can prove challenging for BO (Frazier,, 2018). To circumvent this curse of dimensionality, a wide range of methods have been designed specifically for high-dimensional Bayesian optimization (HDBO), often relying on complex algorithms and strong assumptions on the objective function. We keep a more detailed literature review of these methods for Appendix B, but present the main high-level ideas in this paragraph: common approaches either impose structural assumptions on the objective function, such as an additive decomposition over the input features (Kandasamy et al.,, 2015, e.g.) or sparsity over projected features (Papenmeier et al.,, 2023, e.g.), or reconfigure the BO algorithm to perform local rather than global optimization (Eriksson et al.,, 2019, e.g.). All of these algorithms can be seen as approaches towards reducing the complexity of the objective function or search space.

Dimensionality-Based Smoothness.

A recent line of work by Hvarfner et al., (2024) demonstrates that neither structural assumptions nor explicitly local algorithms are necessary for successful HDBO. Instead, they propose increasing the kernel lengthscale hyperparameters at a rate of D\sqrt{D}—equivalent to re-scaling the 𝒳\mathcal{X} hypercube by 1/D1/\sqrt{D}—to yield an objective function prior that favors smoothness as DD increases. This “Vanilla BO” recipe, alongside contemporaneous methods with similar lengthscale scalings (Xu et al.,, 2025; Papenmeier et al., 2025b, ), significantly outperforms the methods described above on benchmarks with up to D=6000D=6000 dimensions and as few as N=1000N=1000 observations.

Geometric Transformations.

Few works propose geometric warpings of the inputs beyond element-wise scaling through lengthscales. A notable exception is BOCK (Oh et al.,, 2018), who, like us, bijectively map the inputs into a different space before applying a kernel. We note several differences between this method and ours. Superficially, our proposed method maps inputs to a hypersphere, whereas BOCK maps to a hypercylinder. More substantially, our geometric warping is motivated to obtain meaningful performance from linear kernels, whereas BOCK applies this transformation to kernels with high representational capacity.

3 METHOD

The recent works of Hvarfner et al., (2024) and Xu et al., (2025) have demonstrated the necessity of scaling lengthscales with dimensionality, effectively creating a prior that favors increasing smoothness as dimensionality increases. In this work, we investigate if further improvements are possible if we take this smoothness idea to its logical extreme. Importantly, we cannot simply consider a faster rate of lengthscale scaling, as this would lead to ‖𝐱/ℓ−𝐱′/ℓ‖→0\|\mathbf{x}/\ell-\mathbf{x^{\prime}}/\ell\|\to 0 as D→∞D\to\infty, effectively leading to a prior over constant functions. Instead, we turn to what is (under most definitions) the smoothest model of non-constant functions: Gaussian processes with linear kernels.

The idea of using linear kernels (i.e. Bayesian linear regression) for HDBO may appear surprising, especially given that standard BO references discourage its use (Shahriari et al.,, 2015; Garnett,, 2023): the black-box objective functions modeled during BO are often of unknown complexity, necessitating non-parametric and universal approximating surrogates rather than simple parametric models. However, we argue that the limited fidelity of linear models is not a limitation in N≈DN\approx D settings, where there are barely enough observations to “fill up” the capacity of linear models. Instead, we hypothesize that linear kernels can be competitive for HDBO tasks after accounting for pathologies in the optimization geometry.

Below, we propose a modified linear kernel for Bayesian optimization. Like the standard linear kernel, our proposed kernel is rank O⁡(D)O(D) and yields an extremely simple prior over functions. However, as we will demonstrate, our kernel significantly surpasses the BO performance of the standard linear kernel and even rivals the most sophisticated methods.

3.1 Proposed Linear Model

We propose the following linear kernel for GPs (equivalent to Bayesian linear regression):

klinear​(𝐱,𝐱′):=b0+b1​P​(𝐳)⊤​P​(𝐳′),k_{\textrm{linear}}\left(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\right):=b_{0}+b_{1}\;P\left(\mathbf{z}\right)^{\top}P\left(\mathbf{z^{\prime}}\right), (2)

where bi>0b_{i}>0 are hyperparameters, P:ℝD→𝕊DP:\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^{D} is a bijective mapping onto the unit sphere, and 𝐳,𝐳′\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z^{\prime}} are scaled versions of 𝐱,𝐱′\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x^{\prime}}, i.e.

𝐳:=1a​[x1ℓ1⋯xDℓD],𝐳′:=1a​[x1′ℓ1⋯xD′ℓD]\mathbf{z}:=\tfrac{1}{a}\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{x_{1}}{\ell_{1}}&\cdots&\tfrac{x_{D}}{\ell_{D}}\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{z^{\prime}}:=\tfrac{1}{a}\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{x^{\prime}_{1}}{\ell_{1}}&\cdots&\tfrac{x^{\prime}_{D}}{\ell_{D}}\end{bmatrix} (3)

for hyperparameters a∈ℝ+a\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, ℓ∈ℝD\bm{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. Of all the modifications, the spherical mapping is the most impactful (confirmed by ablations in Section D.3). We now define each of these changes more rigorously.

Spherical Mapping.

Linear models induce a boundary-seeking behavior during optimization, which we hypothesize is the primary factor affecting their performance. Specifically, the posterior mean and variance of linear models increase away from the center of the hypercube, resulting in maximal acquisition values on the search space boundary (implicitly discarding most of 𝒳\mathcal{X}). We formalize this idea in the following theorem (see Section A.1 for a proof), and provide a visualization for D=1D=1 in Figure 1.

Theorem 1.

For acquisition functions increasing in posterior mean and variance (e.g. expected improvement), Bayesian linear models will maximize acquisition on the boundary of the search space. That is, for 𝐱t+1=arg⁡max𝐱∈[−1,1]D​αt​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}\in[-1,1]^{D}}\alpha_{t}(\mathbf{x}) at any timestep tt, we have that 𝐱t+1\mathbf{x}_{t+1} contains at least one dimension equal to −1-1 or 11 (i.e. ‖𝐱t+1‖∞=1\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\|_{\infty}=1).

However, when points lie on the unit hypersphere 𝕊D⊂ℝD+1\mathbb{S}^{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D+1} instead of the hypercube [−1,1]D⊂ℝD[-1,1]^{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D}, the acquisition function cannot increase by scaling inputs, since all points are equally far from the origin (i.e. on a sphere) and thus Theorem 1 does not apply (see counterexample in Section A.2). Thus, we propose mapping our inputs 𝐱\mathbf{x} from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to a unit sphere (via PP in Equation 2) before applying the linear kernel.

While numerous mappings from ℝD→𝕊D\mathbb{R}^{D}\to\mathbb{S}^{D} exist, we choose PP to be the inverse stereographic projection:

P⁡(𝐳):=1‖𝐳‖2+1​[2​z1⋯2​zD‖𝐳‖2−1].P(\mathbf{z}):=\tfrac{1}{||\mathbf{z}||^{2}+1}\begin{bmatrix}2z_{1}&\cdots&2z_{D}&||\mathbf{z}||^{2}-1\end{bmatrix}. (4)

As can be seen from the equation, the projection scales all dimensions of the original DD-dimensional vector by their norm (with some constants), and only introduces one additional dimension, resulting in D+1D+1 features for our linear model. This mapping possesses a number of attractive characteristics: it is smooth, bijective over ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D}, and conformal, meaning that it preserves angles at which curves meet (Hilbert and Cohn-Vossen,, 2021). Most notably, it is a (near) identity mapping for unit norm 𝐳\mathbf{z} (i.e. P⁡(𝐳)=[𝐳,0]P(\mathbf{z})=[\mathbf{z},0] when ‖𝐳‖=1\|\mathbf{z}\|=1), a fact we will explore in depth in Section 5.

Decoupled Magnitude and Direction for ℓi\ell_{i}.

To ensure a meaningful distance is maintained between all points as the dimensionality DD grows, recent methods have scaled the lengthscales ℓi\ell_{i} by D\sqrt{D}, either through the hyperprior (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024; Xu et al.,, 2025) or the initialization value (Papenmeier et al., 2025b, ). As a simplified alternative to impose this scaling, we decouple the magnitude and direction of the lengthscale vector. Specifically, we introduce a global lengthscale aa in Equation 3, initialized to be O⁡(D)O(\sqrt{D}), which we multiply by an (unconstrained) vector ℓ\bm{\ell} that models varying sensitivities of each dimension. In the context of our kernel, the O⁡(D)O(\sqrt{D}) scaling on aa ensures that the entries of 𝐳\mathbf{z} are O⁡(1/D)O(1/\sqrt{D}), ensuring our scaled points have O⁡(1)O(1) norm before projecting them onto the unit sphere. We place a log-normal prior on the vector ℓ\bm{\ell}, namely ℓi∼ℒ​𝒩​(2,3)\ell_{i}\sim\mathcal{LN}\left(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3}\right), though we find that performance is largely unaffected by this choice (see Section D.1).

No Implicit Outputscale.

A useful property of RBF kernels is that they are bounded above, i.e. k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)≤1k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\leq 1, achieving the maximum if and only if 𝐱=𝐱′\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^{\prime}. The latter property does not hold for standard linear kernels; however, it is naturally enforced for our spherically-projected inputs. Since PP bijectively maps to the unit hypersphere, we have P​(𝐳)⊤​P​(𝐳′)≤1P(\mathbf{z})^{\top}P(\mathbf{z^{\prime}})\leq 1 and thus klinear​(𝐱,𝐱′)≤b0+b1k_{\mathrm{linear}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\leq b_{0}+b_{1} with equality if and only if 𝐱=𝐱′\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^{\prime}. Inspired by Hvarfner et al., (2024), we further enforce that b0+b1=1b_{0}+b_{1}=1, removing any implicit outputscale that could affect optimization. Since b0,b1>0b_{0},b_{1}>0, we enforce this constraint by learning unconstrained parameters, and then mapping them to the simplex through the softmax function.

3.2 Polynomial Extension

We can naturally extend the logic of our linear kernel to higher-order polynomial kernels via:

kpoly​(𝐱,𝐱′):=∑i=0mbi​[P​(𝐳)⊤​P​(𝐳′)]i,k_{\textrm{poly}}\left(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x^{\prime}}\right):={\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m}b_{i}\left[P\left(\mathbf{z}\right)^{\top}P\left(\mathbf{z^{\prime}}\right)\right]^{i}}, (5)

where m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} indicates the polynomial order. We again constrain the coefficients bib_{i} to the simplex through a softmax function. Kernels of this form are trivially positive semi-definite through a standard application of kernel composition rules (Genton,, 2001, e.g.).

Equation 5 can approximate many kernels on P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′)∈𝕊DP(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})\in\mathbb{S}^{D} to an arbitrary degree of precision. Schoenberg, (1942) proves that any dot-product kernel on the unit sphere (i.e. where the kernel is a function of P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′)P(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})) takes the form of Equation 5 for some value of mm. Moreover, any kernel that is a function of Euclidean distance (e.g. the Matérn or rational quadratic kernels) can be approximated by Equation 5 for inputs P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′)∈𝕊DP\left(\mathbf{z}\right),P\left(\mathbf{z^{\prime}}\right)\in\mathbb{S}^{D} (see Section A.3). For example, Section A.4 shows that the RBF kernel restricted to the unit sphere has the Taylor expansion

kRBF​(P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′))=∑i=0∞1i!​e​[P​(𝐳)⊤​P​(𝐳′)]i.k_{\textrm{RBF}}\left(P\left(\mathbf{z}\right),P\left(\mathbf{z^{\prime}}\right)\right)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{i!\,e}\left[P\left(\mathbf{z}\right)^{\top}P\left(\mathbf{z^{\prime}}\right)\right]^{i}. (6)

Therefore, increasing mm, our proposed model can approximate the RBF kernel (on a hypersphere) with any arbitrary precision. Surprisingly, as will become clear in Section 4.3, there is rarely a need to go beyond m=1m=1 to match state-of-the-art HDBO performance.

3.3 Advantages of Linear Models

Before considering optimization performance, it is worth remarking on the practical benefits afforded by our kernel (or any kernel corresponding to an O⁡(D)O(D) feature expansion), where these benefits cannot be obtained by standard (e.g. RBF or Matérn) kernels.

Computational Scalability.

Since GPs with linear kernels correspond to an O⁡(D)O(D) feature map, we can perform exact posterior inference over the O⁡(D)O(D)-dimensional parameters in O⁡(N​D2)O(ND^{2}) time (Williams and Rasmussen,, 2006). In contrast, RBF and Matérn kernels, which correspond to infinite-dimensional basis expansions, require O⁡(N3)O(N^{3}) computation for exact posterior inference. As a result, linear kernels can be used to scale to optimization problems where N≫DN\gg D (e.g. molecular optimization in Section 4.2), whereas standard kernels require posterior approximations.

Exact Thompson Sampling.

Thompson sampling (Thompson,, 1933), a common acquisition function for high-dimensional problems (Eriksson et al.,, 2019, e.g.) and parallel acquisitions (Hernández-Lobato et al.,, 2017, e.g.), requires sampling a realization of the GP posterior. While standard kernels necessitate approximations or discretizations of 𝒳\mathcal{X} for sampling, linear kernels yield exact posterior function samples. Functions under our linear model posterior can be represented as f⁡(𝐱)=θ0+𝜽⊤​P​(𝐳)f(\mathbf{x})=\theta_{0}+\bm{\theta}^{\top}P(\mathbf{z}), where θ0\theta_{0} and 𝜽\bm{\theta} are (finite-dimensional) Gaussian random variables. Hence, we can exactly sample functions by sampling θ0\theta_{0} and 𝜽\bm{\theta}.

4 EXPERIMENTS

To showcase the performance and scalability of our proposed linear kernel, we evaluate it on a range of optimization problems (both N≈DN\approx D and N≫DN\gg D). Moreover, we ablate the design choices that differentiate our kernel from the standard linear kernel.

Benchmarks.

To test performance in the N≈DN\approx D setting, we evaluate our method on a range of standard benchmarks from the HDBO literature ranging from D=60D=60 all the way to D=6392D=6392: Rover (Wang et al.,, 2018, 60D;), MOPTA08 (Eriksson and Jankowiak,, 2021, 124D;), Lasso-DNA (Nardi et al.,, 2022, 180D;), SVM (Eriksson and Jankowiak,, 2021, 388D;), Ant (Wang et al.,, 2020, 888D;), and Humanoid (Wang et al.,, 2020, 6392D;). We evaluate these tasks under a budget of N=1000N=1000 observations. For the N≫DN\gg D setting, we benchmark on multiple molecular tasks from the GuacaMol benchmark (Brown et al.,, 2019), which typically require large optimization budgets for meaningful progress. We perform BO in the 256D latent space of a pre-trained variational auto-encoder (Maus et al.,, 2022; Maus et al.,, 2024) with a N=20,000N=20,\!000 budget.

Baselines.

For the N≈DN\approx D tasks, we compare against popular HDBO methods: BOCK (Oh et al.,, 2018), TuRBO (Eriksson et al.,, 2019), SAASBO (Eriksson and Jankowiak,, 2021), BAxUS (Papenmeier et al.,, 2022), and “Vanilla BO” (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024), as well as a standard linear kernel as in Equation 1. The N≫DN\gg D tasks necessitate the use of scalable GP approximations (except in the case of linear kernels), and therefore we compare against the EULBO method (Maus et al.,, 2024), which relies on variational approximations. For the “random search” baseline, we perform quasi-random Sobol sampling (Sobol,, 1967) of 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Experimental Set-Up.

Our set-up largely follows Hvarfner et al., (2024): we use the LogEI acquisition function (Ament et al.,, 2023), initialize all methods with 30 quasi-random observations (100100 points for N≫DN\gg D tasks), and follow their other modeling protocols. We run each method for at least 10 different random seeds, and the plots in this paper display the mean and standard error of the mean (with respect to the seeds) as a solid/dotted line and shaded area, respectively. Details of our experimental set-up can be found in Appendix C.

4.1 N≈DN\approx D Optimization Problems

Figure 2 (left) demonstrates optimization performance of all methods on N≈DN\approx D tasks. As expected, the standard linear kernel fails to optimize many benchmarks, though it obtains decent performance on the lower-dimensional tasks. In contrast, our modified linear model matches the current state-of-the-art on all N≈DN\approx D benchmarks. In fact, the optimization trajectories from our linear kernel and Vanilla BO are statistically indistinguishable on the Lasso-DNA and Humanoid benchmarks. We note the stark performance difference between the modified and standard linear kernels on the SVM and Ant datasets. Moreover, in Section E.1, we compare against Vanilla BO on a number of latent-space molecular tasks with a similar observation budget. Spherical linear kernels strongly outperform Vanilla BO on all these benchmarks, potentially suggesting our method is particularly advantageous for latent-space BO.

4.2 N≫DN\gg D Optimization Problems

For N≫DN\gg D molecular tasks, we observe significant performance gains over the scalable EULBO method (Figure 2, right). We hypothesize that our linear kernel, unencumbered by the need for approximations, is better suited for large-NN tasks, despite its lack of representational capacity.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Higher-Order Polynomials.

In Figure 3 (and its extended version, Figure 14, in Section E.2), we replicate the N≈DN\approx D benchmark results for order-mm polynomial kernels of the form in Equation 5. (Recall that our proposed linear kernel is the special case of this form for m=1m=1.) Surprisingly, the polynomial order has almost no effect on optimization performance, with our linear kernel matching the m=5thm=5^{\mathrm{th}} order polynomial on nearly all benchmarks. From a practical perspective, higher order polynomials are net detrimental, as they lose scalability and exact Thompson sampling (the O⁡(Dm)O(D^{m}) feature representation of these kernels is too large to afford these benefits), without improving optimization performance.

Choice of Spherical Mapping.

Our biggest modification to the standard linear kernel is the spherical mapping (see Section 3.1), i.e. the inverse stereographic projection defined in Equation 4. In Figure 4 (and its extended version, Figure 15, in Section E.3), we compare a range of other common mappings from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to the hypersphere (see Section E.3 for descriptions). We also compare against the case of no projection (None), but where we keep our other proposed modifications to the linear kernel (decoupled lengthscales and no implicit outputscale). While we can conclude that a spherical projection is necessary to improve performance, the choice of spherical projection itself can also have a drastic impact on performance.

We note that the inverse stereographic projection, which consistently outperforms all other mappings, is the only mapping that does not modify unit-norm inputs (i.e. P⁡(𝐳)=[𝐳,0]P(\mathbf{z})=[\mathbf{z},0] for all ‖𝐳‖=1\|\mathbf{z}\|=1). We hypothesize that this property may be instrumental in its performance (see Section 5). Interestingly, while a spherical mapping is crucial for linear BO, it has almost no effect for non-parametric models. In Section D.2, we demonstrate that Vanilla BO performance is largely unchanged under the inverse stereographic projection.

Other Ablations.

In Section D.3, we ablate over our other modifications (decoupled lengthscale, centering of the search space, implicit outputscale, etc.), showing that our decoupled parameterization makes our kernel less sensitive to any prior placed on the lengthscale vector ℓ\bm{\ell}. In contrast, priors on standard (coupled) lengthscales have a significant impact on BO performance (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024).

5 ANALYSIS

By conventional wisdom, linear models should not work as well as they do in Section 4. Their success challenges our understanding of what makes effective high-dimensional surrogate models. While our analysis cannot resolve this puzzle, it reveals a tension that may be central to explaining their efficacy. Reconciling the following contradictory observations highlights the non-intuitive nature of HDBO, suggesting that our understanding is fundamentally incomplete:

  1. 1.

    after applying our spherical mapping, the linear kernel exhibits BO behavior that resembles more traditional non-parametric GPs; and yet

  2. 2.

    the spherical mapping is geometrically minor for most points in high dimensional spaces, preserving local structure except at the boundary.

5.1 Spherical Linear Kernels Avoid the Pathologies of Standard Linear Kernels

Standard linear kernels suffer from a pathological limitation in BO: as we prove in Section 3.1, they exclusively acquire points on the boundary of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, implicitly discarding the interior of the search space. We empirically validate this in Figure 5 (left), which plots the percentage of entries of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} equal to ±1\pm 1 for each BO iteration tt under various kernels (0%0\% indicates an interior point and 100%100\% indicates a corner). On the MOPTA08 and SVM tasks, we observe that the standard linear kernel acquires points with 100%100\% of dimensions equal to ±1\pm 1, i.e. corners of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. This represents an even more extreme pathology than simple boundary-seeking: the model restricts itself to the 2D2^{D} corners, a measure-zero subset of both the boundary and the search space (i.e. a finite instead of infinite set of points).

In contrast, RBF kernels acquire points with ≤50%\leq 50\% of entries equal to ±1\pm 1. While these points still lie on the boundary, they are less extreme and cover a broader region of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Our spherically-mapped linear kernel exhibits similar behavior to the RBF kernel, and even yields points entirely in the interior (0%0\% of ±1\pm 1 elements) on the SVM task. (See Section E.4 for plots on additional datasets.) Again, the spherical mapping prevents the monotonic growth in posterior statistics that drives standard linear models toward extremal points (see counterexample in Section A.2).

The Observation Traveling Salesman Distance (Papenmeier et al., 2025a, , OTSD;) measures the minimum path length connecting all acquired points, where lower OTSD values suggest more local search. In Figure 5 (right), standard linear kernels yield large OTSD on MOPTA08 and SVM—often exceeding random search—because corner points (i.e. 100% of dimensions on the boundary) are maximally far apart. In contrast, both our spherically-projected linear kernel and RBF kernels yield similarly low OTSD values, suggesting more local search strategies. (See Section E.5 for plots on additional datasets.) Collectively, these results provide preliminary evidence that spherically-mapped linear kernels exhibit exploration patterns more similar to RBF kernels than to their unmapped linear counterparts, though complete characterization remains future work.

5.2 Spherical and Standard Linear Kernels are Asymptotically The Same

While the spherical mapping P:ℝD→𝕊DP:\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^{D} is crucial for avoiding boundary-seeking pathology, it is a relatively minor transformation for most points in 𝒳\mathcal{X}. The inverse stereographic projection is an identity mapping for unit-norm inputs: P⁡(𝐳)=[𝐳,0]P(\mathbf{z})=[\mathbf{z},0] for all ‖𝐳‖=1\|\mathbf{z}\|=1. When lengthscales are set to 3/D\sqrt{3/D} as suggested by recent work (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024; Xu et al.,, 2025), any 𝐱\mathbf{x} drawn uniformly from 𝒳\mathcal{X} yields a scaled vector 𝐳=[x1/ℓ1,…,xD/ℓD]\mathbf{z}=[x_{1}/\ell_{1},\ldots,x_{D}/\ell_{D}] with ‖𝐳‖→1\|\mathbf{z}\|\to 1 as D→∞D\to\infty—a direct consequence of the law of large numbers (see Section A.5). Thus, for most points in 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the spherically-mapped linear model behaves nearly identically to a standard linear model and has no additional representational capacity.

Moreover, we emphasize that the inverse stereographic projection transforms the DD-dimensional function space into a (D+1)(D+1)-dimensional function space, where this one additional dimension represents less than a 1% increase in DD for most considered benchmarks. In contrast, polynomial kernels rely on a 𝒪⁡(Dm)\mathcal{O}(D^{m})-dimensional function space at a minimum, and RBF or Matérn kernels rely on an ∞\infty-dimensional function space. As a result, although our linear model is technically not linear in 𝐱\mathbf{x} (though it is in P⁡(𝐱)P(\mathbf{x})), we argue it is approximately linear in 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

To validate that the spherical mapping does not meaningfully increase model expressiveness on a typical regression task, we fit both models to 400400 points generated by a Sobol sequence over 𝒳\mathcal{X} and evaluate predictions on 100100 held-out Sobol points (concentrated around unit norm after scaling). In Figure 6 (left), both the spherically-mapped and standard linear models achieve nearly identical predictive RMSE on most benchmarks, while the RBF model generally achieves lower error due to its higher representational capacity (see Figure 18, Section E.6 for results on other benchmarks).

5.3 Model Expressiveness Does Not Predict BO Performance

This similarity on standard regression tasks makes the performance gap in BO (see Figure 2) all the more puzzling: if the spherical and standard linear models have similar predictive capabilities, why do spherical mappings improve optimization so dramatically? The answer is that model expressiveness and predictive accuracy on random test points do not necessarily translate to optimization performance with adaptively chosen data.

To further illustrate this point, Figure 6 (right) repeats the above experiment on adaptively chosen BO acquisitions rather than Sobol points. We fit models to 400400 points from a BO trajectory (generated by our spherical linear model) and predict the objective values at the next 100100 acquired points. In Figure 6 (right) and Figure 18 (right), all three models—spherical linear, standard linear, and RBF—achieve similar predictive accuracy, despite their vastly different performance as BO surrogates (see Figure 18, right, in Section E.6 for results on other benchmarks). These results contrast the supervised learning setting where RBF substantially outperforms linear models on a number of problems.

Why are spherical linear models able to accurately predict future (adaptive) acquisitions but not random test data? One possible explanation is that acquisition functions like EI tend to select points locally (Garnett,, 2023), where objectives may be well-approximated by linear models (i.e. a first-order Taylor approximation) even when globally complex. However, fully characterizing which properties actually matter for HDBO success—beyond standard notions of expressiveness or generalization—remains an important open question.

6 CONCLUSION

In this work, we show that linear models—arguably the simplest of all models—match state-of-the-art performance on high-dimensional BO tasks after mapping inputs to the unit sphere. From a practical perspective, our modified linear kernel also provides state-of-the-art performance on large-NN tasks and promising performance on latent-space tasks. We thus recommend its adoption in these settings. From a theoretical perspective, our findings call into question long-standing intuitions and practices. The fact that linear kernels, largely dismissed by the BO community, achieve such strong performance provides a compelling case against model complexity in high-dimensional settings. We hope that our initial analysis provides the seeds for radically new theories that unlock a new and more robust understanding of high-dimensional BO.

Appendix A Proofs, examples and derivations

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

See 1

Proof.

Most common acquisition functions, including Expected Improvement (EI) and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB), can be shown to be monotonically increasing in the posterior mean μ⁡(𝐱)\mu(\mathbf{x}) and standard deviation σ⁡(𝐱)\sigma(\mathbf{x}) of the underlying surrogate. Now, consider the following proof by contradiction: the acquisition optimum 𝐱\mathbf{x} does not lie on the boundary. If we parametrize 𝐱\mathbf{x} as a direction 𝐳\mathbf{z} and magnitude c≥0c\geq 0, we get

𝐱=∥𝐱∥⏟c⋅𝐱∥𝐱∥⏟𝐳,withμ⁡(𝐱)=𝐱⊤​𝜷^=c⋅𝐳⊤​𝜷^andσ⁡(𝐱)=σε2+𝐱⊤​𝐒𝐱=σε2+c2⋅𝐳⊤​𝐒𝐳.\mathbf{x}=\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert}_{c}\cdot\underbrace{\dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert}}_{\mathbf{z}},\quad\text{with}\quad\mu(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}}=c\cdot\mathbf{z}^{\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}}\quad\text{and}\quad\sigma(\mathbf{x})=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}+\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}}=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}+c^{2}\cdot\mathbf{z}^{\top}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{z}}.

As a result, for any 𝐱\mathbf{x}, increasing cc monotonically increases μ⁡(𝐱)\mu(\mathbf{x}) and σ⁡(𝐱)\sigma(\mathbf{x}), and therefore also α⁡(𝐱)\alpha(\mathbf{x}). Thus, the interior point 𝐱\mathbf{x} cannot be the (constrained) optimum, since increasing cc will result in a higher acquisition value, which is a contradiction and concludes the proof.

Here, we have assumed 𝐱⊤​𝜷^≥0\mathbf{x}^{\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}}\geq 0, since assuming otherwise would lead to a better optimum, namely −𝐱-\mathbf{x}, which is also a contradiction. Moreover, unless all previous data points 𝐱1:t\mathbf{x}_{1:t} obtain exactly the same objective value yy (which is highly unlikely), we can safely assume 𝜷^≠(0,…,0)\hat{\bm{\beta}}\neq(0,\ldots,0), meaning that μ⁡(𝐱)\mu(\mathbf{x}) will be strictly increasing in cc. As a consequence, not only will there be an optimum on the boundary, but this optimum will also be unique, meaning there is no optimum in the interior of the hypercube.

Adding an Intercept

To extend the proof to a Bayesian linear model with an intercept, we follow a similar approach as before, but need to pay closer attention to the parameterization of 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Specifically, we write μ⁡(𝐱)=β^0+𝐱⊤​𝜷^\mu(\mathbf{x})=\hat{\beta}_{0}+\mathbf{x}^{\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}} using the augmented feature map φ⁡(𝐱)=[1;𝐱]\varphi(\mathbf{x})=[1;\mathbf{x}]. The posterior variance can then be expressed as

σ2​(𝐱)=σε2+φ​(𝐱)⊤​𝐒​φ​(𝐱)=σε2+S00+2​𝐱⊤​S0​x+𝐱⊤​Sx​x​𝐱,with𝐒=[S00S0​x⊤S0​xSx​x].\sigma^{2}(\mathbf{x})=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\varphi(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\mathbf{S}\,\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+S_{00}+2\,\mathbf{x}^{\top}S_{0x}+\mathbf{x}^{\top}S_{xx}\mathbf{x},\quad\text{with}\quad\mathbf{S}=\begin{bmatrix}S_{00}&S_{0x}^{\top}\\ S_{0x}&S_{xx}\end{bmatrix}.

Completing the square, we choose a shift point 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} that removes the linear term, i.e. any solution of Sx​x​𝐱0=−S0​xS_{xx}\mathbf{x}_{0}=-S_{0x} (unique when Sx​xS_{xx} is invertible). Then

σ2​(𝐱)=σε2+S00−𝐱0⊤​Sx​x​𝐱0⏟constant in ​𝐱+(𝐱−𝐱0)⊤​Sx​x​(𝐱−𝐱0),\sigma^{2}(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\underbrace{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+S_{00}-\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\top}S_{xx}\mathbf{x}_{0}}_{\text{constant in }\mathbf{x}}\;+\;(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{0})^{\top}S_{xx}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{0}),

where Sx​x⪰0S_{xx}\succeq 0 is the slope block of the posterior covariance.

A.2 Counterexample to Theorem 1 (For Spherical Projections)

We provide a specific example to support the following statement from Section 3.1: “when points are projected to the hypersphere, Theorem 1 does not apply anymore.” That is, for

𝐱t+1=arg⁡max𝐱∈[−1,1]D​αt​(P⁡(𝐱)),\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}\in[-1,1]^{D}}\alpha_{t}\left(P(\mathbf{x})\right),

where P:ℝD→𝕊DP:\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^{D}, the optimum 𝐱t+1\mathbf{x}_{t+1} can be any point in the hypercube (i.e. ‖𝐱t+1‖∞∈[0,1]\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\|_{\infty}\in[0,1]), instead of only boundary points (i.e. ‖𝐱t+1‖∞=1\|\mathbf{x}_{t+1}\|_{\infty}=1) as stated in Theorem 1.

For simplicity, consider D=1D=1 and UCB with an exploration factor of λ=0\lambda=0, giving us

αt​(P⁡(x))=P​(x)⊤​𝜷^,where we assume𝜷^=(1/2−1).\alpha_{t}(P(x))=P(x)^{\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}},\quad\text{where we assume}\quad\hat{\bm{\beta}}=\begin{pmatrix}\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}\\ -1\end{pmatrix}.

As spherical mapping P:ℝD→𝕊DP:\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^{D}, we consider the inverse stereographic projection from Equation 4, giving us

α⁡(x)=12⋅2​xx2+1−x2−1x2+1,withα⁡(−1)=−12,α⁡(12)=1,α⁡(1)=12.\alpha(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+1}-\dfrac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+1},\quad\text{with}\quad\alpha(-1)=-\tfrac{1}{2},\quad\alpha\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=1,\quad\alpha(1)=\tfrac{1}{2}.

Here, the interior point x=1/2x=\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} leads to a higher acquisition value than the two boundary points x=−1x=-1 and x=1x=1, thus representing a clear example for which Theorem 1 does not hold (because of the non-linear projection P⁡(x)P(x) from the real line ℝ\mathbb{R} to the circle 𝕊\mathbb{S}).

A.3 Isotropic Kernels Become Dot-Product Kernels (After Spherical Projection)

Any isotropic kernel becomes a dot product kernel when applied to unit norm inputs.

Let k:ℝ∞×ℝ∞→ℝk:\mathbb{R}^{\infty}\times\mathbb{R}^{\infty}\to\mathbb{R} be an isotropic kernel, where ℝ∞×ℝ∞\mathbb{R}^{\infty}\times\mathbb{R}^{\infty} denotes that the kernel is valid on any possible input dimensionality. By the result of Schoenberg, (1938, Theorem 2), this kernel can be expressed as:

k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)=∫exp⁡(−ℓ2​‖𝐱−𝐱′‖22)​𝑑μ​(ℓ)=∫exp⁡(−ℓ⁡(‖𝐱‖2+‖𝐱′‖2)2)​exp⁡(ℓ​𝐱⊤​𝐱′)​𝑑μ​(ℓ)k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\int\exp\left(-\frac{\ell}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right)d\mu(\ell)=\int\exp\left(-\frac{\ell\left(\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|^{2}\right)}{2}\right)\exp\left(\ell\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)d\mu(\ell) (7)

where μ⁡(ℓ)\mu(\ell) is some positive finite measure over [0,∞)[0,\infty). Without loss of generality, we assume that μ\mu is a probability measure—alternatively, we can normalize the measure by 1/μ⁡([0,∞))1/\mu([0,\infty))—as the value of μ⁡([0,∞))\mu([0,\infty)) can be viewed as an implicit outputscale on the kernel.

Applying this kernel to sphere-projected inputs P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′)P(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}) (which are both unit norm), we have:

k⁡(P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′))=∫exp⁡(−ℓ)​exp⁡(ℓ​P​(𝐳)⊤​P​(𝐳′))​𝑑μ​(ℓ)k(P(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}))=\int\exp\left(-\ell\right)\exp\left(\ell P(\mathbf{z})^{\top}P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})\right)d\mu(\ell)

Taking a Taylor expansion of the right exponential and applying Fubini-Tonelli, we have:

k⁡(P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳′))=∑i=0∞∫ℓi​exp⁡(−ℓ)​𝑑μ​(ℓ)i!​[P​(𝐳)⊤​P​(𝐳′)]i.k(P(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}))=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{\int\ell^{i}\exp\left(-\ell\right)d\mu(\ell)}{i!}\left[P(\mathbf{z})^{\top}P(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})\right]^{i}. (8)

As ℓi​exp⁡(−ℓ)\ell^{i}\exp\left(-\ell\right) is trivially bounded for any i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} and ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0, the integrals in Equation 8 are all finite and well defined. Furthermore, by Equation 7 we have that k⁡(P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳))=1k(P(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}))=1 for all 𝐳\mathbf{z}; combining this fact with Equation 8 we have that

k⁡(P⁡(𝐳),P⁡(𝐳))=∑i=0∞∫ℓi​exp⁡(−ℓ)​𝑑μ​(ℓ)i!=1.k(P(\mathbf{z}),P(\mathbf{z}))=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{\int\ell^{i}\exp\left(-\ell\right)d\mu(\ell)}{i!}=1. (9)

In other words, the polynomial coefficients sum to 1, and thus kk restricted to the unit sphere can be arbitrarily approximated by the higher order polynomial kernel in Equation 5.

A.4 Derivation of Equation 6

The polynomial expression of the sphere-based RBF kernel can be derived from Equations 7 and 8, under the atomic measure d​μ​(ℓ)=δ⁡(ℓ−1)d\mu(\ell)=\delta(\ell-1), where δ\delta is the Dirac delta function.

A.5 Thin Shell Phenomenon

Assume X=(X1,X2,…,XD)X=(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{D}) is generated uniformly over the DD-dimensional hypercube [−1,1]D[-1,1]^{D}. Moreover, define the scaled variables ZZ as Z=[X1/ℓ1⋯XD/ℓD]=X​3/DZ=\begin{bmatrix}X_{1}/\ell_{1}&\cdots&X_{D}/\ell_{D}\end{bmatrix}=X\sqrt{3/D}, where the lengthscales have been scaled according to O⁡(D)O(\sqrt{D}) as suggested in recent works (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024; Xu et al.,, 2025; Papenmeier et al., 2025b, ). Then, we have

𝔼⁡(Xi2)=12​∫−11xi2​𝑑x=13,andvar​(Xi2)=12​∫−11xi4​𝑑x−𝔼​(Xi2)2=445,\mathbb{E}\left(X_{i}^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}x_{i}^{2}\,dx=\frac{1}{3},\quad\text{and}\quad\textrm{var}\left(X_{i}^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}x_{i}^{4}\,dx-\mathbb{E}\left(X_{i}^{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{4}{45},

which gives us

𝔼⁡(Zi2)=1D,andvar​(Zi2)=45​D2.\mathbb{E}\left(Z_{i}^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{D},\quad\text{and}\quad\textrm{var}\left(Z_{i}^{2}\right)=\frac{4}{5D^{2}}.

Using the above, we have

𝔼⁡(‖Z‖2)=∑i=1D𝔼⁡(Zi2)=1,andvar⁡(‖Z‖2)=∑i=1Dvar​(Zi2)=45​D.\mathbb{E}\left(\|Z\|^{2}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\mathbb{E}\left(Z_{i}^{2}\right)=1,\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{var}\left(\|Z\|^{2}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\textrm{var}\left(Z_{i}^{2}\right)=\frac{4}{5D}.

Therefore, as D→∞D\rightarrow\infty, it follows that

𝔼⁡(‖Z‖2)=1,andvar⁡(‖Z‖2)=0,\mathbb{E}\left(\|Z\|^{2}\right)=1,\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{var}\left(\|Z\|^{2}\right)=0,

meaning ‖Z‖\|Z\| converges to 1 (in probability, and almost surely). This phenomenon is also known more broadly as the “thin shell phenomenon”, and we refer the reader to Vershynin, (2025) for a more complete treatment of the topic.

Appendix B Extended Related Work

Low-Dimensional Subspaces

Instead of searching in a high-dimensional space, a major stream of HDBO methods instead map 𝒳\mathcal{X} to a low-dimensional subspace, on which the search is more feasible. This mapping can be: (i) linear, with methods such as REMBO (Wang et al.,, 2016), HeSBO (Nayebi et al.,, 2019), ALEBO (Letham et al.,, 2020), BAxUS (Papenmeier et al.,, 2022), and Bounce (Papenmeier et al.,, 2023), or (ii) non-linear, with methods such as DMGPC-BO (Moriconi et al.,, 2020) and LOL-BO (Maus et al.,, 2022). Additionally, the linear embeddings can be focused on variable selection only, as done in Dropout-Mix (Li et al.,, 2017), SAASBO (Eriksson and Jankowiak,, 2021), MCTS-VS (Song et al.,, 2022), and GTBO (Hellsten et al.,, 2025).

Local Search

Alternatively, instead of performing global search in a low-dimensional subspace, another stream of methods instead perform local search in the full-dimensional space. This can be done using: (i) trust regions, such as TuRBO (Eriksson et al.,, 2019), CASMOPOLITAN (Wan et al.,, 2021), and CTS-TuRBO (Rashidi et al.,, 2024), or (ii) approximate gradients, such as GIBO (Müller et al.,, 2021; Wu et al.,, 2023), MPD (Nguyen et al.,, 2022), and LA-MinUCB (Fan et al.,, 2024).

Additive Decompositions

Rather than change the search space, additive-decomposition methods impose simplifying assumptions on the structure of the objective function. Examples include Add-GP-UCB (Kandasamy et al.,, 2015), G-Add-GP-UCB (Rolland et al.,, 2018), Tree-GP-UCB (Han et al.,, 2021), and RDUCB (Ziomek and Ammar,, 2023).

Appendix C Implementation Details

We run EULBO (Maus et al.,, 2024) and BAxUS (Papenmeier et al.,, 2022) using the authors’ original implementations. For TuRBO (Eriksson et al.,, 2019), SAASBO (Eriksson and Jankowiak,, 2021), and Vanilla BO (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024), we use implementations present in BoTorch (Balandat et al.,, 2020). For BOCK (Oh et al.,, 2018), we replicate the authors’ original implementation as closely as possible using the provided kernel in GPyTorch (Gardner et al.,, 2018), allowing for an easy integration with BoTorch.

Due to the high computational costs associated with SAASBO, we only run the model for 500 iterations, whereas all other methods are run for 1000 iterations. We run each method for at least 10 different random seeds, and the plots in this paper display the mean and standard error of the mean (with respect to the seeds) as a solid line and shaded area, respectively. We run our linear kernel as well other baselines on a cluster containing both CPUs and GPUs, where the latter were used to speed up computation for slower methods or datasets. Vanilla BO and our proposed linear kernel delivered similar run times (±10%\pm 10\%): given an evaluation budget of N=1000N=1000, the pipeline takes between 1h and 12h on 1 NVIDIA GPU (e.g. L40S) depending on the benchmark. For the molecular experiments with N>N>\penalty\ 20,000 (on a similar GPU), the pipeline takes between four and six days.

Appendix D Additional Ablation Studies

D.1 Effect of Hyperprior

As mentioned in Section 3.1, performance of our linear model is largely unaffected by the hyperprior placed on the lengthscales. In Figure 7, we evaluate three different hyperpriors:

  1. 1.

    Gamma: ℓi∼Γ⁡(3,6)\ell_{i}\sim\Gamma(3,6), which used to be the default in BoTorch (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024),

  2. 2.

    LogNormal: ℓi∼ℒ​𝒩​(2+log⁡(D)2,3)\ell_{i}\sim\mathcal{LN}\left(\sqrt{2}+\frac{\log(D)}{2},\sqrt{3}\right), which is used in Vanilla BO (often referred to as DSP), and

  3. 3.

    LogNormal*: ℓi∼ℒ​𝒩​(2+log⁡(1)2,3)\ell_{i}\sim\mathcal{LN}\left(\sqrt{2}+\frac{\log(1)}{2},\sqrt{3}\right), which is equivalent to DSP without the dimensionality DD, since scaling by DD is not needed when combined with our global lengthscale aa (see Section 3.1).

As can be seen, using Gamma instead of LogNormal* leads to identical performance for our linear model (orange and red lines), whereas it results in large differences when applied to standard RBF kernels (green and purple lines). In the following section, we discuss how our proposed spherical projection and global lengthscale can be combined with RBF kernels (brown and pink lines).

D.2 Effect of Our Spherical Mapping on an RBF Kernel

In Section 4.3, we claim that the inverse stereographic projection has almost no effect for non-parametric models. To support this claim, we evaluate the RBF kernel on points projected to the unit hypersphere; see the left-hand side of Equation 6 for a more explicit formulation. In Figure 7, this RBF kernel applied to the hypersphere (brown line) leads to similar performance as the RBF kernel from Vanilla BO (green line), supporting our claim above. Moreover, replacing the LogNormal prior from Vanilla BO by the Gamma prior (pink line) does not degrade performance for our model (thanks to our projection and global lengthscale aa), whereas it does lead to significantly worse results for the standard RBF kernel (Hvarfner et al.,, 2024, as presented in).

D.3 Effects of Projection, Centering, ARD, and Global Lengthscale

In Figure 8, we modify certain components of our model proposed in Section 3.1 and assess their impact on performance. We consider four modifications: (i) no spherical projection PP (i.e. PP is an identity map), (ii) a non-centered search space [0,1]D[0,1]^{D} (instead of [−1,1]D[-1,1]^{D}), (iii) no Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) for the lengthscales (i.e. replacing ℓi\ell_{i} by ℓ\ell), and (iv) removing the global lengthscale aa (i.e. a=1a=1).

As confirmed by Figures 4 and 15, the spherical projection is the most important element among our different modifications, and removing it significantly affects performance. Similarly, going from a centered hypercube [−1,1]D[-1,1]^{D} to a non-centered hypercube [0,1]D[0,1]^{D} leads to a noticeable drop in performance. We hypothesize that this is related to the inverse stereographic projection, where the “0-boundary” and the “1-boundary” are treated differently if we don’t center, but exactly the same if we do. Specifically, Equation 4 heavily relies on the norm of 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and both boundaries will have different norms if no centering is applied. Interestingly, though both our global lengthscale and ARD bring performance improvements, these improvements are rather minor in contrast to centering and spherical projection of the search space.

D.4 Effect of Acquisition Function

Our results do not change significantly if we replace EI with UCB (Figure 9): Vanilla BO and our proposed linear model obtain performance similar to that in Figure 2. If we replace EI with TS (Figure 10), both methods incur a noticeable performance drop. However, our spherical linear model still matches, and sometimes exceeds, the performance of an RBF GP with TS (i.e. Vanilla BO). For the generation of the Thompson samples, we rely on Wilson et al., (2020), which means we can optimize the acquisition function using gradient-based methods.

D.5 Effect of Problem Structure

Here we test our linear models versus Vanilla BO models on synthetic problems with known objective functions. In particular, we aim to assess the relative efficacy of our method as we increase the degree of sparsity and nonlinearity in the objective.

Effect of Sparsity.

Following the setup in Hvarfner et al., (2024, Figure 5), we embed the Levy (D=4D=4) and Hartmann (D=6D=6) functions into a range of higher dimensionalities (D=25D=25, D=100D=100, D=300D=300, and D=1000D=1000), thus leading to objective functions with increasing amounts of sparsity (Levy and Montalvo,, 1985; Hartman,, 1973). For both test functions, we observe a clear trend across dimensionality (Figure 11): as the embedding dimension grows (i.e. sparsity increases), the gap between Vanilla BO and our proposed linear model vanishes. From these results, we conclude that our proposed linear model might be more suited to functions with a higher dimensionality or a higher degree of sparsity.

Effect of Non-Linearity in the Objective Function.

We consider objective functions that are varying convex combinations of linear and non-linear objective functions. Specifically, we draw the objective function from a Gaussian process with the following kernel:

ktest=α​klinear+(1−α)​kRBF,withα∈[0,1].k_{\textrm{test}}=\alpha\,k_{\textrm{linear}}+(1-\alpha)\,k_{\textrm{RBF}},\quad\text{with}\quad\alpha\in[0,1]. (10)

Small values of α\alpha correspond to highly nonlinear functions; large values correspond to nearly linear functions. In Figure 12, as α\alpha goes from zero to one, the difference between our proposed linear model and Vanilla BO vanishes (30% gap to 5% gap). Nevertheless, we observe that our spherical linear model still yields substantial optimization progress even when the objective function is entirely nonlinear (α=0\alpha=0).

Appendix E Complete Experimental Results

E.1 GuacaMol Datasets for N=1,000N=1,\!000

We compare our linear kernel from Equation 2 against Vanilla BO on nine different tasks from the GuacaMol benchmark (Brown et al.,, 2019). Specifically, we run both methods in the 256D latent space of the SELFIES-VAE (Maus et al.,, 2022), and plot the results in Figure 13. On all nine datasets, our linear model significantly outperforms Vanilla BO, potentially indicating (a part of) its design is better suited for (molecular) latent spaces. We leave more thorough analysis of this strong performance to further work, but believe it to be a fruitful direction.

E.2 Higher-Order Polynomials

We replicate the results of Figure 3 in Figure 14, where the latter now contains six datasets instead of two. The conclusions for this extended figure are the same as in Section 4.3: higher-order polynomials (m>1m>1) from Equation 5 all obtain near-identical performance compared to the linear kernel (m=1m=1). The only (minor) exception to this rule is the MOPTA08 dataset, where higher-order polynomials slightly outperform the linear kernel.

E.3 Choice of Spherical Mapping

We extend the findings from Figure 4 in Figure 15, which expands the analysis to encompass six datasets rather than two. In both figures, we rely on our linear kernel from Equation 2, and only modify the spherical projection PP. Here, None means no projection is used (i.e. PP is an identity map), the Inverse stereographic projection is defined in Equation 4, and the remaining projections can be written as:

Pradial​(𝐳)\displaystyle P_{\textrm{radial}}(\mathbf{z}) =1γ​[z1⋯zDγ2−‖𝐳‖2],\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\gamma}\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}&\cdots&z_{D}&\sqrt{\gamma^{2}-||\mathbf{z}||^{2}}\end{bmatrix},
Pnorm.​(𝐳)\displaystyle P_{\textrm{norm.}}(\mathbf{z}) =1‖𝐳‖​[z1⋯zD],\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{||\mathbf{z}||}\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}&\cdots&z_{D}\end{bmatrix},
Phomo.​(𝐳)\displaystyle P_{\textrm{homo.}}(\mathbf{z}) =1‖𝐳‖+D​γ​[z1⋯zDγ1⋯γD],\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{||\mathbf{z}||+D\gamma}\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}&\cdots&z_{D}&\gamma_{1}&\cdots&\gamma_{D}\end{bmatrix},
P(co)sine​(𝐳)\displaystyle P_{\textrm{(co)sine}}(\mathbf{z}) =1‖𝐳‖​[z1​cos⁡(‖𝐳‖)⋯zD​cos⁡(‖𝐳‖)z1​sin⁡(‖𝐳‖)⋯zD​sin⁡(‖𝐳‖)],\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{||\mathbf{z}||}\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}\cos\left(||\mathbf{z}||\right)&\cdots&z_{D}\cos\left(||\mathbf{z}||\right)&z_{1}\sin\left(||\mathbf{z}||\right)&\cdots&z_{D}\sin\left(||\mathbf{z}||\right)\end{bmatrix},

where γ=γ1=…=γD\gamma=\gamma_{1}=\ldots=\gamma_{D} represents the largest norm possible for 𝐳\mathbf{z} (given that 𝐳\mathbf{z} is a scaled version of 𝐱∈[−1,1]D\mathbf{x}\in[-1,1]^{D}).

This broader comparison of datasets yields consistent conclusions with those presented in Section 4.3: a spherical projection is necessary to improve performance, but the choice of spherical projection can have a drastic impact on performance. For example, simple Normalization achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Ant dataset, but is outperformed by all other projections—including no projection at all—on the MOPTA08 dataset. For the final version of our linear kernel, we opt for the Inverse stereographic projection, which consistently delivers superior performance across datasets.

E.4 Percentage of Dimensions on the Boundary

In Figure 16, we complement the results of Figure 5 by adding four more datasets (for a total of six). As described in Section 5, we can clearly observe a corner-seeking behavior for the standard linear kernel, with almost 100%100\% of the dimensions (of acquired points) lying on the boundary. For our linear kernel and Vanilla BO, this is not the case, but we note a surprisingly high diversity of acquired points across datasets: from almost 0%0\% dimensions on the boundary for SVM and Ant to more than 50%50\% for the other four datasets.

E.5 Observation Traveling Salesman Distance (OTSD)

Similar to the above paragraph, we expand the results of Figure 5 in Figure 17 to include four more datasets. Here, we can observe a similar pattern as described in Section 5: the corner-seeking behavior of the standard linear kernel leads to an OTSD metric often exceeding that of random search, whereas our spherically-mapped linear kernel displays patterns of “locality” closer to those of Vanilla BO. Additionally, we can see that the OTSD metric for the standard linear kernel keeps increasing with dimensionality DD. This result is not surprising: as DD grows large, corners in a high-dimensional hypercube are increasingly far away from each other compared to randomly-sampled points.

E.6 Regression Performance

In Figure 18, we add four more datasets (for a total of six) to the Box plots of Figure 6. Based on these six datasets, we draw the same conclusions as in Section 5:

  1. 1.

    the points chosen during the BO loop are easier to predict than evenly-spread Sobol points (perhaps because of the “local” behavior of our model), and

  2. 2.

    our spherically-mapped linear model does not significantly improve the regression performance of the standard linear model (thus discarding the idea that the performance of our linear model is due to strong, non-linear features induced by the spherical projection).
